# Dynamic Navigation and Metadata in PHP Includes Splitting your HTML into `head.php`, `footer.php`, and `navbar.php` is a standard pattern for maintaining consistency across a site. However, simply including these files statically leaves you with two critical problems: every page looks identical because the navigation lacks context, and you cannot easily swap out titles or meta descriptions without repeating code. To solve this, you need to decouple the static structure from the dynamic content. The most robust approach in plain PHP is to pass data into your include files using variables defined in the main script. ## Passing Dynamic Data via Variables The cleanest way to handle page-specific titles and meta descriptions is to define a variable array or individual variables at the top of your main file (e.g., `index.php`) before including the header. Here is how you might structure `index.php`: ```php ``` You must then modify `head.php` to accept these variables. Since you cannot pass arguments directly into a file included via `include()` without modifying the function signature, the standard practice is to check for variables defined in the parent scope or wrap the include logic in a helper function. A more maintainable pattern involves creating a dedicated view file that expects specific variables: ```php <?php echo $page_title; ?> ``` This approach avoids the "spaghetti code" of trying to inject arguments into raw `include()` statements. It keeps your include statements clean while allowing full control over metadata. ## Highlighting Active Navigation Links The navigation bar presents a slightly different challenge because it requires knowledge of the current URL to determine which link should display the `active` class. You cannot rely solely on variables passed from the top of the file; you need to inspect the request context. In the included `navbar.php`, you can use PHP's built-in functions to compare the current script name against your menu links. ```php 'index', 'Page 1' => 'page1', 'FAQ' => 'faq', ]; $current_page_name = basename($_SERVER['PHP_SELF']); ?>

``` ### Handling the "Index" Edge Case A common pitfall here is how PHP handles `index.php`. If your user visits `https://yoursite.com/` (without a file extension), `$_SERVER['PHP_SELF']` might return just `/`. However, if they visit `https://yoursite.com/index`, it returns `/index`. To make the active state reliable regardless of how the user types the URL, you should normalize the current path. You can use `basename()` on `$_SERVER['REQUEST_URI']` and strip query strings before comparison. This ensures that whether a user clicks "Home" or types the URL directly, the correct list item receives the Bootstrap `active` class. ## Trade-offs of Static Includes While this variable-passing method works well for small to medium sites, it introduces a maintenance burden as your project grows. Every time you add a new page, you must: 1. Update the `$nav_items` array in `navbar.php`. 2. Create a corresponding entry in your main file to define the title and description. If you forget to update one of these, your site will either break or display incorrect metadata. This tight coupling between your routing logic (which files exist) and your layout logic (how they are displayed) is why frameworks like Laravel were built. They automate this exact pattern, ensuring that when you create a route for "Contact", the controller automatically updates the view with the correct title and highlights the correct navigation link without manual intervention. For larger applications, consider migrating to an MVC framework where these concerns are handled by routing and view composers rather than raw PHP includes.
